427.t: Prohibition: pitchers of whiskey, police pay-offs and staged raids
427.s: Whiskey was fetched across the street in pitchers; police were paid off but raided for show, and everyone was taken to jail and released.
427.q: You'd have to throw the whiskey out. Had a tub back there with a lot of Lysol in it, an' you throw it in the Lysol, and [ ] flashing lights. Had a man 'cross the street, one on each corner, who watched for the coppers, and when they see the coppers comin', he would flash the lights, so the lights…

427.t: Bootleg half-pints from his mother's flat and the monthly printer
427.s: With friends he sold bootleg whiskey from the empty flats his mother managed, and recalls a printer who came each month on a bender.
427.ch: Black and Tan and Kansas City nightlife
427.q: I got so I'd go out on Twelfth Street. We used to have...we moved up to another flat when Momma was the manager of it, and we had a...always kept maybe one or two apartments empty. So, we got so a bunch of us fellows got together, and we had a...a joint. We sold whiskey. Bootleg whiskey. We sell it…

427.t: Buying and pricing corn liquor, burnt-sugar 'red' and needle whiskey
427.s: The Italians delivered whiskey by phone; prices, how white was made red, and the effect of needle whiskey.
427.ch: Black and Tan and Kansas City nightlife
427.q: We bought it from the I-talians. If you'd have a automobile...if you had an old Ford--that's all they drove is Fords--and happens if you call the cat who delivers the whiskey. He deliver whiskey all over town to all them plants and after-hours joints and places all over town.

710.s: Bailey describes making home brew; the interviewers mention Shots Madison selling it in Prohibition.
710.q: No, we used to make it too, at all. I don't know. We'd make it, put it up, and have to leave it for four or five days, then you go to put it in your bottle. You get a cap, then after you put it in the bottle, you leave it there for about... Well, some folks leave it for a day, and then they go to…

710.s: Speakeasies were quiet hole-in-the-wall places; Bailey tells how an undercover policeman caught his uncle.
710.q: Well, yeah, you get sometime in them speakeasies. Used to have a place called in the Barney to be speakeasy. You have to know them horses to go in and knock at. Yeah. They get in. Yeah, because they're Stricon. Speakeasy.

1.t: Chicken Cock whiskey in a can
1.s: Danny and Smitty bought canned Chicken Cock whiskey at the Mad House, which was thrown overboard from rum-runners' boats.
1.ch: Arriving in New York: the Nest Club and Harlem nightlife
1.q: But that was a wild street. Smitty and I used to come upstairs some mornings... We'd go in the Nest Club. When we'd have a break, then we'd come upstairs and go in the Mad House, and we would buy Chicken Cock Whiskey, which was whiskey that came in a can.

1.t: Sour mash dumped on Federal Street
1.s: Racketeers dumped sour mash from their stills in the vacant lots where the boys played.
1.ch: Chicago, Lee Collins and the road
1.q: And we'd play all up in Federal Street, and we'd play up in the lots up in there, and had this big pile of corn, about seven feet high. A big dump truck we saw come in the morning and dump this corn. We wondered what it was. It was sour mash that the racketeers were making at the still. Instead of…

663.t: Whiskey, food and bootleggers at country parties
663.s: Musicians were paid in whiskey; bootleggers sold beer and fried chicken at parties.
663.q: Oh, yeah, man. Shit. Oh, man. He said, uh, plenty of food like us.

254.t: Spanish Fort, West End and a prohibition raid
254.s: They discuss outings to Spanish Fort and the lake, and Mrs. Clementin tells of a prohibition agent with a missing hand arriving at a camp.
254.ch: Reel 2: carnival, Prohibition, funerals and clubs
254.q: I used to do the last time they put them in the water, the camps out there. They had a great ground fall, you know, when the water, people go swimming. Every Sunday, every barn house is packed.

251.t: Third reel opening and chalk beer
251.s: Allen opens the third reel on Aug 6, 1973 and asks about chalk, a homemade beer drunk in speakeasies.
251.ch: Later years and the Texas scene
251.q: Well, you mean Chalk, you talking about Chalk the beer? Yeah. Oh yeah, I thought you were talking about somebody's name. That's the beer we used to drink, Chalk beer. That's a homemade beer, homebrew. It was in the speakeasers.

118.s: Fish fries without permits, speakeasies in prohibition and the origin of the term, then a harmonica question.
118.q: Oh, we played fish fry down. Plenty of fish fry. Oh, man. That's good days, fish fry. And what made it so nice, you know what I mean? You hear the police come and you have to jump the back fence.

15.t: Gunmen, 1919 police shootings and musicians in gang-era clubs
15.s: Howard tells about the shootings of two policemen in 1919, newspapers and how musicians stayed out of it.
15.q: You know, in gang war. You know how they do. Were they pretty big time? Well they must have been, because they didn't, not one of them served a day for that. They show you what kind of town Chicago it was. The papers, it was on a Sunday morning. I'm pretty sure it was on a Sunday morning. They come…

323.t: Prohibition, speakeasies and drinking with Howard Tifft
323.s: Speakeasies and spiked beer as a teenager; a night out drinking with pianist Howard Tifft.
323.q: That is right. There were speakeasies. That’s right. You had to knock on the door and — spiked beer. You know? Near beer, and then they put the alcohol in, a hundred percent, oh my goodness.

400.t: Teenage work in his uncle's cleaning shop selling Capone's bootleg whiskey
400.s: Al Capone supplied alcohol to Hinton's uncle Pete Ford, who resold it for house rent parties; Hinton cut the bonded strips and pressed suits as a front.
400.ch: Capone's Chicago, the union and hired by Cab
400.q: Well Al Capone, he organized Chicago. He came from New York, from Brooklyn. He came to Chicago to be a bodyguard for Jim Colisemo and Jim Colisemo was killed in a room that had no windows in it [laugh] and Al Capone was the bodyguard and of course Al Capone took over after that. Then he took over.…

80.t: Bessie's sister and bootleg liquor in the alley
80.s: Her sister sold corn liquor on Catur Street, and the family had a Chattanooga riverboat scheme of hiding jugs under the water.
80.ch: Mutes, influences and the blues singers
80.q: No, not between she and I no, but I saw her -- I knew her sister. Her sister lived in Catur Street, down at the beginning of Catur Street. She had several children, and we used to go in there and buy our liquor. This was during prohibition, you know, days, and she

113.t: Arkansas City as a bootleg town and the staged raids
113.s: He describes Arkansas City, Kansas, drawing patrons from dry Oklahoma and Kansas, and how raids were tipped off in advance and soon forgotten.
113.ch: Leaving home: Fisk, Tulsa, Arkansas City
113.q: Well, what made that lively -- you see, there was a lot of people that used to come down there from Winfield, Kansas. Winfield is about 18 or 20 miles north of there and there was a lot of people that come up from Oklahoma and there was Newkirk, Oklahoma, Ponca City, Oklahoma. These little towns.…

67.t: Rent parties, buffet flats and home-made gin
67.s: Chicago rent parties served chitlins, bootleg whiskey and gambling, and raids were frequent; Cheatham avoided buffet flats.
67.ch: Chicago clubs, entertainers and tent shows
67.q: Rent parties and card games. Performers and musicians would meet all the time. And apartments, and where the bootleg whiskey was sold and cards and gambling, that's where a lot of the people made their money to pay their rent.

93.t: High hat and tails: minstrels, the crash and Prohibition
93.s: Green explains how minstrels popularised top hat and tails, which Harlem blacks wore only on special occasions until the end of Prohibition and nightlife made them fashionable.
93.q: Well, in a way they were, because the blackface -- the minstrels had popularized the high hat and tails, because they was all considered doctors, you see. Remember minstrel shows, they had these -- they called themselves medicine shows, and they -- with the minstrels, you see. And they -- I think…

6.t: Prohibition raids, gambling and buffet flats
6.s: He was never in a raided place; he explains buffet flats as apartments where you could buy a drink, and the bootleg gin sold in them.
6.ch: Early records, Detroit and Prohibition-era nightlife
6.q: No, that's one thing, all my career, I was never in a place that was raided, never. They used to raid the -- in fact they'd raid most anyplace when they got ready. Even the Musicians' Club they used to raid. On any trumped up excuse, because they used to have gambling in the back room and all that.…

86.t: Cleveland speakeasies and the whiskey hose at Valsen Alley
86.s: Cleveland flourished on underworld money and speakeasies, and Edison describes the waiter serving whiskey from a rubber bag.
86.ch: Jeter-Pillars in Cleveland and St. Louis
86.q: Well, you know, wherever there's a lot of underworld, there's a lot of money. And at that time there was a lot of speakeasies, you know, where you could go buy whiskey, you know. And the town was flourishing because there was all those illegitimate clubs you could go to and people were having more…

171.t: Dry Kansas and wide-open Missouri; John Brown's caves
171.s: Musicians lived in dry Kansas and played in wide-open Missouri; Western University sat on John Brown's route.
171.ch: Western University and Kansas City nightlife
171.q: Yeah. Well, Kansas was completely dry. And it wasn't, I guess, until about '32 that they had even three or four percent beer --you know, something like that. Anyway, it was something that was non-intoxicating, you know.

112.t: Harlem rent parties and Buffet Flats
112.s: He says he was above rent parties and describes Buffet Flats with pianolas, liquor in teapots and rooms upstairs, and landlords favouring madams.
112.q: And they didn't have any piano players, but they had the pianolas. Put a Lucky Roberts piano roll on, Peter Wedling. And some of the other fellows that had made rolls for the piano roll companies. And then you set there and drink. Because it was prohibition. And they would serve you the liquor in a…
